# Load test (generated by `loadtest/run_loadtest.sh`)

Run 2026-11-23 22:56 UTC with k6 0.54 against the live stack through nginx (the same path a browser uses). Each virtual user behaves like an open console: `/api/state` every second (ETag), recommendations and alerts every 3 s, system status every 5 s. The simulator keeps running and the engine keeps planning during the test.

## Read load: api ×1 vs ×3

| VUs | x1 p50 ms | x1 p95 ms | x1 req/s | x1 errors | x3 p50 ms | x3 p95 ms | x3 req/s | x3 errors | engine ticks behind (max) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 25 | 5.3 | 105.7 | 43 | 0.00% | 3.8 | 47.5 | 46 | 0.00% | 0 / 0 |
| 50 | 4.6 | **210.5** | 89 | 0.00% | 4.0 | 98.6 | 90 | 0.00% | 0 / 0 |
| 100 | 9.3 | **500.8** | 157 | 0.00% | 4.4 | **220.7** | 173 | 0.00% | 0 / 0 |
| 200 | 391.3 | **1092.7** | 211 | 0.00% | 6.3 | **492.1** | 314 | 0.00% | 0 / 0 |
| 400 | 1195.6 | **2605.7** | 220 | 0.00% | 213.7 | **1219.9** | 438 | 0.00% | 0 / 0 |

**Knee** (first load level where p95 > 200 ms): api ×1: 50; api ×3: 100.

## Spike: 10 → 300 VUs in 5 s (api ×3)

p50 2.7 ms · p95 17.7 ms · 344 req/s · errors 0.00% · engine ticks behind (max) 0

## Rate limit (normal configuration: 600 requests/min per client)

One client (k6, 20 VUs, no sleep) fired 17,745 requests in 15 s: every response was 200/304 or **429**, **zero 5xx**.
The 700 requests that followed from the same client were all 429 (its minute was already spent), each with
`Retry-After: 60`. The limit is per client IP (the rightmost `X-Forwarded-For` entry, set by our nginx, so it cannot be
forged) and shared by all api replicas through Redis.

## Before / after: optimizing the hot path

The first run (same script, same machine) found the api's limits; we then changed `/api/state`:
the engine publishes a **content-hash ETag** next to the document, the api compares it **before** reading the document
(304 without touching the 11.7 KB body), otherwise returns the cached bytes **as they are** (no JSON parse and
re-serialize), and the rate limiter uses **one** Redis round trip (Lua) instead of two.

| Measure | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Spike 10 → 300 VUs, `/api/state` only, api ×3: p95 | 96.8 ms | **17.7 ms** |
| api ×1 at 200 VUs: p95 / throughput / errors | 3,800 ms / 113 req/s / 1.5 % | **1,093 ms / 211 req/s / 0 %** |
| api ×1 at 100 VUs: p95 | 618 ms | **501 ms** |
| knee (p95 > 200 ms), api ×1 / ×3 | 50 / 200 VUs | 50 / 100 VUs |

Honest reading: the hot path got 5× faster and the overload errors are gone, but the knee did not move. With a p50 of
4-9 ms, the p95 tail comes from the heavier, less frequent console calls (`/api/system/status` asks the engine; alerts
and recommendations are separate documents) on a replica limited to **0.5 CPU**. Scaling out is what moves the knee
(×3 replicas: 2-4× more load at the same latency), and the engine stayed at **0 ticks behind in every run**.

The same work also fixed a correctness bug: the old ETag was `run-tick`, but mode, data age and health change within a
tick (during an outage the tick stops), so browsers revalidating with `If-None-Match` could keep getting 304 and miss
SAFE_HOLD. The content hash makes that impossible (`services/api/tests/test_state_api.py`).

## Why the engine does not notice
The api is stateless and serves the state document the engine publishes to Redis (with a content-hash ETag, so unchanged content costs a 304). Operator traffic never reaches the engine or the simulator, so decision freshness (`fsip_ticks_behind`) is independent of API load: a bulkhead by design.

Reproduce: `make up && make obs-up && bash loadtest/run_loadtest.sh`.
